V. COMPUTATIONAL HARDNESS OF THE CLASSICAL SAMPLING PROBLEM
A. General overview of the computational complexity argument
B. The partition function for random circuits
Appendix A: Residual correlations after discrete errors

figures.shows: A random quantum circuit on a 1D array of five qubits, each starting in |0>, with a Hadamard layer, controlled-phase (CZ) gates drawn as vertical lines, single-qubit gates T, X^1/2 and Y^1/2, and a measurement on each qubit at the right.
figures.confirmed_by: A circuit, corresponding to a unitary transformation U , is a sequence of d clock cycles of one- and two-qubit gates

figures.shows: Distribution function Pr(Np) (y, log scale, 10^-4 to 10^1) of rescaled output probabilities Np (x, 0 to 10). Blue r = 0 curve follows the Porter-Thomas form (blue dots); curves for r = 0.001, 0.002, 0.005 and 0.01 become narrower and end at smaller Np as r grows; a dashed line marks Np = 1.
figures.confirmed_by: approaches the exponential form N e−Np, known as Porter-Thomas [3], see Fig. 2.

figures.shows: Np (y, 0 to 14) against p-ordered bit-string index j (x, from 1 to N). Blue 'No errors' line rises from about 0 to about 14 at the last index; red 'One Pauli error (averaged)' line stays near about 1 with noise.
figures.confirmed_by: even one Pauli error completely destroys the state [57], as seen in numerical data in Fig. 3.

figures.shows: Circuit fidelity alpha (y, 0 to 1) against number of qubits (x, about 16 to 50) for r = 0, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.002 and 0.005; circular markers are simulated fidelities (Eq. 19), square markers are cross entropy differences; a red vertical line at 48 qubits and a blue horizontal line at alpha = 0.1.
figures.confirmed_by: We observe a good agreement between these two quantities.

figures.shows: Probability distribution Pr_alpha(log(N pU(x))) (y, 0 to about 0.6) against log(N pU(x)) (x, -5 to 3) as step histograms with dashed theory curves; four curves labelled alpha = 1, 0.61, 0.29 and 0 in the legend.
figures.confirmed_by: We ﬁnd a good ﬁt between this expression and numerical simulations, see Fig. 5.

figures.shows: Eight panels (1 to 8) of dots on a 6 x 6 qubit lattice, each panel marking which neighbor pairs hold a CZ gate in that layout.
figures.confirmed_by: Place controlled-phase (CZ) gates alternating between eight conﬁgurations similar to Fig. 6.

figures.shows: Mean output entropy (y, main 26.0 to 29.5; inset 22.5 to 25.0) against depth (x, 0 to 30) for 7 x 6 qubits (main) and 6 x 6 qubits (inset), with a dashed line at the Porter-Thomas entropy and error bars.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 7 shows the output distribution entropy as a function of circuit depth.

figures.shows: Normalized inverse participation ratios IPR(k) N^(k-1)/k! (y, log scale, 10^1 to 10^19) against depth (x, 5 to 30) for k = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with 7 x 6 qubits; inset zooms depths 25 to 30 (y, 0.98 to 1.08); all curves approach 1.
figures.confirmed_by: This is evidenced in Fig. 8 for moments up to k = 10 with circuits consisting of 7 × 6 qubits.

figures.shows: First depth at which entropy stays within 4-sigma of Porter-Thomas (y, 20 to 36) against number of qubits (x, 15 to 45), mean markers with standard-deviation error bars, rising from about 21.6 at 16 qubits to about 33 at 42 qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: These data indicates that the required depth to achieve this criteria grows sublinearly in n.

figures.shows: Two-dimensional histogram of correlation after a single Z error (y, 0 to 1) against depth of the error (x, 1 to 40); color is counts (0 to 20). Nearly all counts sit at correlation about 0, with some weight near correlation about 1 only at depths of about 35 to 40.
figures.confirmed_by: We see that a phase-ﬂip does not aﬀect the output distribution if it is applied close to the end of the circuit.

figures.shows: Two-dimensional histogram of correlation after a single X error (y, 0 to 1) against depth of the error (x, 1 to 40); color is counts (0 to 20). Most counts sit at correlation about 0; weight near correlation about 1 appears at the first depths and at depths of about 35 to 40.
figures.confirmed_by: Bit-ﬂip errors do not have any eﬀect after the cycle of Hadamards at the beginning of the circuit (see Sec. IV), which rotate the initial state (in the computational basis) to the x basis.

figures.shows: Time per single-qubit Hadamard gate (y, 0 to 30 s) against qubit position where the gate is applied (x, 26 to 42) for 34, 38 and 42 qubits; labels 42 qubits 1.18 GB/s, 38 qubits 4.0 GB/s, 34 qubits 4.8 GB/s; time jumps above position 30.
figures.confirmed_by: For example, for a 42-qubit system on 4,096 sockets, the time to apply a Hadamard gate to qubit 41 is 29 seconds – a nearly threefold increase compared to applying a Hadamard gate to qubit 31.

figures.shows: Simulator performance for five random circuits (5 x 4, 6 x 4, 6 x 5, 6 x 6, 7 x 6; 20 to 42 qubits) at optimization levels no spec, spec, spec+cb: percent of gates needing communication, sockets, fused gates, average time per gate, and time for depth 25 (0.039 s for 20 qubits up to 989.0 s for 42 qubits at spec+cb).
figures.confirmed_by: Table I compares simulator performance characteristics of ﬁve random circuits with diﬀerent lattice dimensions and number of qubits.

figures.shows: Treewidth upper bound (y, about 20 to 55) against depth (x, 25 to 50) for 6 x 6, 7 x 6 and 7 x 7 qubits; all rise with depth, 7 x 7 highest.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 13 shows numerical upper bounds for the treewidth as a function of depth for the circuits in Sec. IV.

figures.shows: Total number of T gates (y, 0 to 250) against depth (x, 0 to 40) for 6 x 6, 7 x 6 and 7 x 7 qubits, rising roughly linearly to about 170, about 203 and about 237 at depth 40.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 14 plots the number of T gates.

figures.shows: First layer after which entropy stays within 4-sigma of Porter-Thomas (y, 14 to 24) against number of qubits (x, 15 to 45) for the denser circuits of Appendix E, from about 15 at 16 qubits to about 21 at 42 qubits, non-monotonic in between.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 15 shows the ﬁrst layer of each random circuit instance for which the entropy remains within 4-sigma of the Porter-Thomas entropy during all the following layers

papers.what_it_is: Google-led theory and simulation paper proposing random-circuit sampling with a cross entropy difference as a near-term quantum supremacy benchmark, with supercomputer simulations of up to 42 qubits and a complexity argument for classical hardness.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum supremacy as achieved when a formal computational task is performed with an existing quantum device which cannot be performed using any known algorithm running on an existing classical supercomputer in a reasonable amount of time.
quotes: Quantum supremacy is achieved when a formal computational task is performed with an existing quantum device which cannot be performed using any known algorithm
computer in a reasonable amount of time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition of quantum supremacy in Section I.

assertions.value: The authors study the task of sampling from the output distributions of (pseudo-)random quantum circuits, which they call a natural task for benchmarking quantum computers.
quotes: We study the task of sampling from the output distributions of (pseudo-)random quantum circuits, a natural task for benchmarking quantum computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the computational task the paper studies.

assertions.value: The authors report supercomputer simulations of circuits with up to 42 qubits, which they describe as the largest quantum circuits simulated to date for a computational task that approaches quantum supremacy.
quotes: modeling circuits with up to 42 qubits - the largest quantum circuits simulated to date for a computational task that approaches quantum supremacy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study, with a priority claim as of the paper's date.
assertions.reader_inference: Appendix D of the same paper says a later simulator (Ref. 90) reports 45 qubits, so the priority claim is dated to this paper.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, while chaotic states are extremely sensitive to errors, quantum supremacy can be achieved in the near-term with approximately fifty superconducting qubits.
quotes: We argue that while chaotic states are extremely sensitive to errors, quantum supremacy can be achieved in the near-term with approximately ﬁfty superconducting qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's argument and projection, not a proved or measured result.

assertions.value: The authors state that state-of-the-art supercomputers cannot simulate universal random circuits of sufficient depth in a 2D lattice of approximately 7 × 7 qubits with any known algorithm and significant fidelity.
quotes: State-of-the-art supercomputers cannot simulate universal random circuits of suﬃcient depth in a 2D lattice of approximately 7 × 7 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the limits of known classical algorithms.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself simulated only up to 42 qubits; the 7 x 7 statement rests on the cost estimates in Sections II and VI.

assertions.value: The authors report good convergence of the first ten moments and the entropy of the output distribution to the Porter-Thomas distribution at depth 25 with circuits of up to 7 × 6 qubits in a 2D lattice.
quotes: We study numerically the convergence of the output distribution to the PorterThomas distribution, characteristic of quantum chaos.
We ﬁnd a good convergence for the ﬁrst ten moments and the entropy at depth 25 with circuits of up to 7 × 6 qubits in a 2D lattice.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ratio of probabilities in Eq. (1), an experimentally observable quantity, is enormously sensitive to the effective per-gate error rate r, where g, proportional to n d, is the total number of gates.
quotes: where the parameter r provides an estimate of the eﬀective per-gate error rate, and g ∝ nd is the total number of gates
Therefore, the ratio of probabilities in Eq. (1), an experimentally observable quantity, is enormously sensitive to the eﬀective per-gate error rate r.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim from an argument given later; not a stated theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the distribution of measurement probabilities of a state produced by a random quantum circuit approaches the exponential form known as Porter-Thomas.
quotes: approaches the exponential form N e−Np, known as Porter-Thomas [3], see Fig. 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes the form to Porter and Thomas (Ref. 3) and supports it with its own simulation in Fig. 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the output of a random quantum circuit cannot be distinguished from a uniform sampler unless the specific output probabilities are pre-computed.
quotes: a random quantum circuit can not be distinguished from a uniform sampler over {xj} unless we pre-compute the
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's statement for samples of size polynomial in n, with references only.

assertions.value: The authors state in a footnote that the 1 norm distance between the Porter-Thomas distribution and the uniform distribution over the output bit-strings is 2/e, independent of n.
quotes: Speciﬁcally, the 1 norm distance between the Porter-Thomas distribution and the uniform distribution over {xj } is 2/e, independent of n.
Therefore, information theoretically, a constant small number of measurements are suﬃcient to distinguish these distributions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value stated in a footnote without derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the circuit depth needed to approach the Porter-Thomas regime is expected to correspond to the ballistic spread of entanglement, a timescale that grows as n1/D (exponent printed flat) where D is the dimension of the qubit lattice.
quotes: This timescale grows as n1/D where D is the dimension of the qubit lattice.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited expectation from the chaos literature, not tested at this point in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors measure the quality of an algorithm A for a given number of qubits n as the difference between its cross entropy and the cross entropy of a uniform classical sampler, and call this quantity the cross entropy difference.
quotes: We will measure the quality of an algorithm A for a given number of qubits n as the diﬀerence between its cross entropy and the cross entropy of a uniform classical sampler.
We call this quantity the cross entropy diﬀerence:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition in Section II.B.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cross entropy difference is unity for the ideal random circuit if the entropy of the output distribution equals the entropy of the Porter-Thomas distribution, and zero for the uniform distribution.
quotes: This quantity is unity for the ideal random circuit if the entropy of the output distribution is equal to the entropy of the Porter-Thomas distribution, and zero for the uniform distribution, see Eqs. (3) and (8).
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the definition of the cross entropy difference and the entropy and cross entropy values derived in Section II.A; the condition (entropy equal to Porter-Thomas) is in the quote.

assertions.value: The authors state that in Section V they extend the method used to show the computational hardness of sampling commuting random circuits (IQP) to the general case of universal random circuits.
quotes: In this section we will extend the method used to show the computational hardness of sampling commuting random circuits (IQP) [23, 29] to the general case of universal random circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own complexity argument.

assertions.value: The authors cite the Stockmeyer Counting Theorem as stating that probabilistically approximating the number of solutions Wx, and therefore q(x), to within a multiplicative factor can also be performed with an NP oracle.
quotes: An important result in computer science, the so-called Stockmeyer Counting Theorem [63], states that probabilistically approximating the number of solutions Wx, and therefore q(x), to within a multiplicative factor, can also be performed with an NP oracle, see App. F.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Stockmeyer (Ref. 63).

assertions.value: Appendix F outlines the Stockmeyer Counting Theorem as stating that an NP-oracle also suffices to determine, with high probability, an approximation q˜(x) to the number of solutions q(x) of Eq. (F1), with |q˜(x) − q(x)| < q(x)/poly(n), where poly(n) denotes any chosen polynomial in n.
quotes: The Stockmeyer Counting Theorem states that an NP-oracle also suﬃces to determine, with high probability, an approximation q˜(x) to the number of solutions q(x) of Eq. (F1)
|q˜(x) − q(x)| < q(x)/poly(n)
where poly(n) denotes any chosen polynomial in n.
assertions.certainty_reason: An outline of a theorem the paper attributes to other work (Refs. 63, 92, 93), not proved here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the probability of success of the hash-function algorithm can be amplified to 1 − 1/(4κ) with κ invocations of the NP-oracle.
quotes: The probability of success can be ampliﬁed to 1 − 1/(4κ) with κ invocations of the NP-oracle.
assertions.certainty_reason: Part of an outline of a cited theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is a strongly held conjecture in computational complexity theory that probabilistically approximating partition functions with purely imaginary temperatures is much harder, in the worst case, than any problem which can be solved by an NP oracle.
quotes: These intuitive arguments are supported by the strongly held conjecture in computational complexity theory that probabilistically approximating partition functions with purely imaginary temperatures is much harder, in the worst case, than any problem which can be solved NP oracle [23, 25, 64].
assertions.certainty_reason: A conjecture the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, if an approximate classical sampling algorithm for pU existed with asymptotic complexity polynomial in n and small distance in the 1 norm, and if a sufficiently large fraction of the resulting Ising instances is conjectured to be as hard to approximate as the worst case, then such an efficient classical sampling cannot be achieved.
quotes: Assume now that there exists an approximate classical sampling algorithm for the distribution pU with asymptotic complexity polynomial in n and small distance in the 1 norm.
If we conjecture that a suﬃcient large fraction of these instances is as hard to approximate as the worst case, we must conclude that such an eﬃcient classical sampling cannot be achieved.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conditional argument that rests on a conjecture and on numerically found Porter-Thomas convergence, not a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The 1 norm is the l1 norm; the symbol was lost in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that pU(x) can be mapped directly to the partition function of a quasi three-dimensional random Ising model, with no apparent structure that makes it easier to approximate than a random instance.
quotes: We will show in the next section that pU (x) can be mapped directly to the partition function of a quasi three-dimensional random Ising model, with no apparent structure that makes it easier to approximate than a random instance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The mapping is derived in Section V.B, but the 'no apparent structure' part is an author's judgment.

assertions.value: The authors state that the amplitude of a bit-string can be viewed as a Feynman path integral with individual paths formed by a sequence of the computational basis states of the n-qubit system.
quotes: The expression (24) can be viewed as a Feynman path integral with individual paths {σ−1, σ0, . . . , σd} formed by a sequence of the computational basis states of the n-qubit system.
assertions.certainty_reason: A representation derived in Section V.B; the theorem-level statement and conditions are not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the wavefunction amplitudes take the form of a partition function of a classical Ising model with energy Hs for a state s and purely imaginary inverse temperature iπ/4.
quotes: One can see from comparing (26) with (27)-(29) that the wavefunction amplitudes x|ψd take the form of a partition function of a classical Ising model with energy Hs for a state s and purely imaginary inverse temperature iπ/4.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation for the specific circuit family of Section IV; not a labelled theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that for r ≥ 1 the distribution of the Ising coupling coefficient Jikjl decays exponentially with r.
quotes: for r ≥ 1 the distribution Pr[Jikjl = r] decays exponentially with r
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived distribution under the assumptions stated in Section V.B for a random layout, not a labelled theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the coupling graph of the Ising model represents a quasi three-dimensional structure formed by worldlines corresponding to qubits.
quotes: represents a quasi three-dimensional structure formed by worldline corresponding to qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: A structural summary of a derivation under stated assumptions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the very strong cancellation in the partition-function sum prevents any efficient algorithm from being able to accurately estimate the amplitude.
quotes: This very strong cancellation prevents any eﬃcient algorithm from being able to accurately estimate the quantity
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; no theorem statement with conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the near future quantum computers without error correction will be able to approximately sample the output of random quantum circuits which state-of-the-art classical computers cannot simulate.
quotes: In the near future, quantum computers without error correction will be able to approximately sample the output of random quantum circuits which state-of-the-art classical computers cannot simulate [20–30].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's projection.

assertions.value: The authors state that if an experimental quantum device achieves a cross entropy difference surpassing the performance of the state-of-the-art classical competition, this will be a first demonstration of quantum supremacy.
quotes: If an experimental quantum device achieves a cross entropy diﬀerence surpassing the performance of the state-of-the-art classical competition, this will be a ﬁrst demonstration of quantum supremacy [31].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about a proposed test.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cross entropy can be measured up to the quantum supremacy frontier with the help of supercomputers, after which it can be extrapolated by varying the number of qubits, the number of non Clifford gates and/or the circuit depth.
quotes: The cross entropy can be measured up to the quantum supremacy frontier with the help of supercomputers.
After that point it can be extrapolated by varying the number of qubits, the number of non Cliﬀord gates [48], and/or the circuit depth [45, 46].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's proposal, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum supremacy can be claimed if the theoretical estimates are in good agreement with the experimental extrapolations.
quotes: Quantum supremacy can be claimed if the theoretical estimates are in good agreement with the experimental extrapolations.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's proposed criterion, stated as a recommendation.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study the cost of all the listed classical simulation algorithms and conclude that, with state-of-the-art supercomputers, they fail for universal random circuits with more than approximately 48 qubits and depth ∼ 40.
quotes: We study the cost of all these algorithms and conclude that, with state-of-theart supercomputers, they fail for universal random circuits with more than approximately 48 qubits and depth ∼ 40.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from cost estimates, as of 2016-2017.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own simulations reach 42 qubits; beyond that the cost conclusion is an estimate.

assertions.value: Following previous works, the authors argue that, under certain assumptions, there does not exist an efficient classical algorithm which can sample the output of a random quantum circuit with a constant error (in the 1 norm) in the limit of a large number of qubits n.
quotes: we argue that, under certain assumptions, there does not exist an eﬃcient classical algorithm which can sample the output of a random quantum circuit with a constant error (in the 1 norm) in the limit of a large number of qubits n
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument under stated assumptions, not a proved result.

assertions.value: The authors state that achieving a constant error in the limit of large n requires a fault tolerant quantum computer, which will not be available in the near term.
quotes: Unfortunately, achieving a constant error in the limit of large n requires a fault tolerant quantum computer, which will not be available in the near term
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the asymptotic hardness argument themselves.
assertions.reader_inference: This limits how far the asymptotic hardness argument covers a near-term device.

assertions.value: The authors state that it has been argued, also using computational complexity theory, that the exact output distribution of certain quantum circuits with a constant probability of error per gate is also asymptotically hard to simulate classically.
quotes: Nonetheless, it has been argued, also using computational complexity theory, that the exact output distribution of certain quantum circuits with a constant probability of error per gate is also asymptotically hard to simulate classically [73].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. 73.

assertions.value: The authors state that a specific figure of merit and an accurate error model are absent from previous experimental results with quantum systems which can not be simulated directly.
quotes: This is absent from previous experimental results with quantum systems which can not be simulated directly
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's characterization of prior work.

assertions.value: The authors note that the numerical simulation and experimental curves in Ref. [74] are reasonably well fitted by a rescaled cosine, and so can be approximately extrapolated efficiently classically.
quotes: Furthermore, we note that the numerical simulation and experimental curves in Ref. [74] are reasonably well ﬁtted by a rescaled cosine.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's observation about a cited experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that a device which qualitatively outperforms state-of-the-art classical computers in the random-circuit sampling task is clearly not simply a device simulating itself.
quotes: A device which qualitatively outperforms state-of-the-art classical computers in this task is clearly not simply a device
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that their proposal based on experimental measurements of the cross entropy represents a novel way of characterizing and validating digital error models, and open quantum system theory in general.
quotes: Our proposal based on experimental measurements of the cross entropy, represents a novel way of characterizing and validating digital error models, and open quantum system theory in general.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim of novelty.

assertions.value: The authors state that estimating the circuit fidelity by directly measuring the cross entropy is a fundamentally new way to characterize complex quantum circuits.
quotes: Estimating the circuit ﬁdelity by directly measuring the cross entropy (see Eq. (14)) is a fundamentally new way to characterize complex quantum circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim of novelty.

assertions.value: The authors report that a phase-flip does not affect the output distribution if it is applied close to the end of the circuit, because the computational basis in which they measure is insensitive to phase errors.
quotes: We see that a phase-ﬂip does not aﬀect the output distribution if it is applied close to the end of the circuit.
The reason is that we measure in the computational basis, which is insensitive to phase errors.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one circuit, with a stated reason.

assertions.value: The authors report that bit-flip errors do not have any effect after the cycle of Hadamards at the beginning of the circuit, which rotate the initial state (in the computational basis) to the x basis.

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one circuit.
